messages.author: f42b0240615306ac
messages.subject: Optimize a negative binomial model
parts:
Dear Stan,

I am implementing a simple negative binomial model using the neg_binomial_2 function in Stan. A simplified version of my model is attached. I have 2 questions: (1) can I speed up the model by optimizing the code? (2) Is it necessary to transform the expected mean in exponential (y ~ neg_binomial_2(exp(mu), phi))? This is equivalent to modeling the log-transformed y. How would this transformation affect the estimation?

Thanks much,

Xulong

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Optimize a negative binomial model
parts:
Take a look at

y ~ neg_binomial_2_log(eta, phi)

(note the _log suffix) which is equivalent to

y ~ neg_binomial_2(exp(eta), phi)

Thanks Michael,

Not surprising the neg_binomial_2_log function takes twice as much time as the neg_binomial_2 function, because of the extra exponential transformation. I do not see a necessity for using neg_binomial_2_log at the moment. I will stick with neg_binomial_2.

Xulong

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Optimize a negative binomial model
parts:
It should be faster than exponentiating yourself. That's
the usual (inverse) link function for negative binomial or
Poisson.

You can't log-transform the y, because it's discrete.

You need to supply a positive argument to negative_binomial()
or negative_binomial_log().

- Bob

Hi Bob,

I was not trying to log-transform the y. I was only choosing between to exponentiate the expected mean or not to. But thanks for the reminds.

I am using negative_binomial_2(mu, phi) at the moment, while mu is the expected mean and phi is the precision. I set the lower bounds of mu and phi as 0 and a very flat cauchy prior: cauchy(0, 10). I need to set the lower bounds of both mu and phi as a small positive number as you pointed. But does Stan has some mechanism to take care of this issue? I feel it is not neat to set the lower bounds as some arbitrary positive number.

parts:
> On Apr 30, 2015, at 3:04 PM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Bob,

> I was not trying to log-transform the y. I was only choosing between to exponentiate the expected mean or not to. But thanks for the reminds.

> I am using negative_binomial_2(mu, phi) at the moment, while mu is the expected mean and phi is the precision. I set the lower bounds of mu and phi as 0 and a very flat cauchy prior: cauchy(0, 10). I need to set the lower bounds of both mu and phi as a small positive number as you pointed. But does Stan has some mechanism to take care of this issue? I feel it is not neat to set the lower bounds as some arbitrary positive number.

It's OK to set lower bounds to 0 on things that should
be positive --- the only way it gets to 0 is by underflow.

You can bound it away from 0 with a hard constraint, but
we've been recommending more informative priors.

- Bob
